glossary.unverplant.title: Unassigned
glossary.unverplant.short: The part of your income that has no job yet: income minus expenses minus buffer allocations. The goal is 0.
glossary.unverplant.text: Unassigned is the amount not yet distributed in a month. It is income − expenses − allocations to buffers (plus any carry-over from the previous month and withdrawals into the budget). If it is positive, give the money a job – for example, fill a buffer or pay off debt faster. If it is negative, you have planned more than you have.
glossary.zerobased.title: Zero-based budgeting
glossary.zerobased.short: Every euro gets a job in advance – until “Unassigned” is exactly 0.
glossary.zerobased.text: With zero-based budgeting you plan every month in advance and distribute all income across expenses, savings and debt repayment until nothing is left unassigned. It is the opposite of a pure expense tracker that only records afterwards where the money went.
glossary.regel503020.title: 50/30/20 rule
glossary.regel503020.short: Rule of thumb: 50% of income for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for saving and paying off debt.
glossary.regel503020.text: The 50/30/20 rule splits net income into three groups: needs (housing, mobility, living costs, minimum payments), wants (leisure, treats, giving) and savings (reserves, investing, extra repayments). The statistics show how your actual split deviates from these targets – from 5 percentage points you get a hint.
glossary.polster.title: Buffer
glossary.polster.short: A savings pot for a purpose, e.g. emergency fund, vacation or car repairs – separate from the running budget.
glossary.polster.text: A buffer is a pot you allocate money to, regularly or once. Every allocation reduces Unassigned in that month. Buffers can have a target; progress shows balance ÷ target. Withdrawals are possible up to the current balance and are documented with date and reason.
glossary.notgroschen.title: Emergency fund
glossary.notgroschen.short: A reserve for the unexpected. Recommendation: about three months of net income.
glossary.notgroschen.text: The emergency fund protects you from unexpected expenses like a broken washing machine or losing your job. As a starting value BudgetPlaner suggests three months of income. The buffer traffic light counts how many months of expenses your emergency fund covers (green from three months).
glossary.zuweisung.title: Allocation
glossary.zuweisung.short: Money you give to a buffer. It reduces Unassigned by exactly this amount.
glossary.zuweisung.text: An allocation increases a buffer’s balance by exactly the amount and reduces Unassigned in the same month. Plan regular allocations as a savings plan; they are booked automatically on the due date.
glossary.entnahme.title: Withdrawal
glossary.entnahme.short: Taking money out of a buffer – at most up to the current balance, always with a reason.
glossary.entnahme.text: For a withdrawal you choose whether the money flows into the budget (increases Unassigned, e.g. to pay a repair) or was spent directly (only reduces the balance). The history shows date, amount and reason.
glossary.sparplan.title: Savings plan
glossary.sparplan.short: A regular allocation to a buffer, e.g. 200 every month.
glossary.sparplan.text: A savings plan is a recurring budget item of type “buffer allocation”. It is booked automatically on the debit day and feeds into the savings goal forecast.
glossary.ampel.title: Traffic light system
glossary.ampel.short: Green, yellow or red show at a glance how healthy an area is – always with icon and text.
glossary.ampel.text: Budget, account balance, debts, buffers and the 50/30/20 groups each have a traffic light. Example budget: Unassigned ≥ 0 is green, below −10% of income red, in between yellow. Clicking the light shows the calculation. The household owner can adjust the thresholds.
glossary.cashflow.title: Cash flow
glossary.cashflow.short: When money arrives in your account and when it leaves – day by day in the calendar.
glossary.cashflow.text: The cash-flow calendar shows inflows, outflows and the running balance for every day. Days with a negative balance are marked critical. This way you spot bottlenecks before they happen – for example when rent is debited before your salary arrives.
glossary.kontostand.title: Balance check
glossary.kontostand.short: Your actual account balance on a day. It is the starting point for the balance history and forecast.
glossary.kontostand.text: As BudgetPlaner works without a bank connection, you enter your balance yourself from time to time. From this check the app calculates day by day. Differences between calculated and actual balance are shown.
glossary.rhythmus.title: Payment rhythm
glossary.rhythmus.short: How often an item occurs: monthly, every 2 months, quarterly, half-yearly, yearly or one-time.
glossary.rhythmus.text: Non-monthly items appear in the budget only in their due month. The start month sets the cycle (e.g. yearly in March). In the statistics you can additionally spread them proportionally (“smoothed”) across all months.
glossary.abbuchungstag.title: Debit day
glossary.abbuchungstag.short: The day of the month a payment is due. It sets the position in the cash-flow calendar.
glossary.abbuchungstag.text: Days beyond the end of the month (e.g. the 31st in February) fall on the last day of the month. Without a fixed day the item counts at the start of the period.
glossary.fixkosten.title: Fixed and variable costs
glossary.fixkosten.short: Fixed costs are constant and contractual (rent, insurance). Variable costs fluctuate (groceries, fuel).
glossary.fixkosten.text: The distinction helps with planning: fixed costs can hardly be changed in the short term, variable costs can. The fixed-cost ratio shows how much of your income is already committed.
glossary.fixkostenquote.title: Fixed-cost ratio
glossary.fixkostenquote.short: Fixed expenses ÷ income. Above 60% it gets tight – then you get a warning.
glossary.fixkostenquote.text: A high fixed-cost ratio means little room for the unexpected and for saving. Review contracts, subscriptions and insurance policies.
glossary.sparquote.title: Savings rate
glossary.sparquote.short: Share of income that is saved: savings expenses + buffer allocations − withdrawals, divided by income.
glossary.sparquote.text: The statistics show the savings rate per month and, from the third month on, a rolling 3-month average. A benchmark is 20% according to the 50/30/20 rule.
glossary.ueberschuss.title: Surplus
glossary.ueberschuss.short: Income minus expenses – before buffer allocations.
glossary.ueberschuss.text: The surplus shows how much is left after all expenses. It is then distributed to buffers or remains “unassigned”.
glossary.uebertrag.title: Carry-over
glossary.uebertrag.short: The remainder of a closed month that was taken over into the next month.
glossary.uebertrag.text: When closing a month you decide what happens with the remainder: carry it over, allocate it to a buffer or drop it. A carry-over appears as its own line in the next month and increases (or reduces) Unassigned.
glossary.monatsabschluss.title: Month closing
glossary.monatsabschluss.short: Freezes the values of a month. Closed months are read-only and form the basis for statistics.
glossary.monatsabschluss.text: When closing, you review open items, distribute the remainder and optionally record the account balance at month end. A closed month can be reopened at any time.
glossary.monatsstart.title: Month start day
glossary.monatsstart.short: The day your budget month starts – e.g. the 25th, when your salary arrives.
glossary.monatsstart.text: With a start on the 25th, “November” starts on 25 October and ends on 24 November. Changes only affect future months; the transition month is extended or shortened automatically.
glossary.sollist.title: Planned and actual
glossary.sollist.short: Planned is the budgeted amount, actual what really happened. Without an entered actual, actual = planned.
glossary.sollist.text: You can check off every item each month and enter the actual amount if it differs. The statistics then show per category where you are above or below plan. Spot on means a deviation of 0.
glossary.restschuld.title: Remaining balance
glossary.restschuld.short: The amount you still have to repay.
glossary.restschuld.text: The remaining balance drops with every payment by the principal share. At 0 the debt is automatically marked as paid off.
glossary.tilgung.title: Principal
glossary.tilgung.short: The part of a payment that actually reduces the debt (payment minus interest).
glossary.tilgung.text: For a loan with interest every payment consists of an interest and a principal share. Without an interest rate the whole payment counts as principal.
glossary.zinsanteil.title: Interest share
glossary.zinsanteil.short: The part of a payment that goes to the creditor as interest: remaining balance × rate ÷ 12.
glossary.zinsanteil.text: Because the remaining balance shrinks over time, the interest share gets smaller and the principal share larger – with a constant payment.
glossary.annuitaet.title: Annuity loan
glossary.annuitaet.short: A loan with a constant monthly payment of interest and principal.
glossary.annuitaet.text: The time to become debt-free follows from remaining balance, interest rate and payment. If the payment does not even cover the interest, the debt grows – then no forecast is possible.
glossary.sondertilgung.title: Extra repayment
glossary.sondertilgung.short: A payment on top of the regular one. It goes entirely towards principal and saves interest.
glossary.sondertilgung.text: Plan a monthly extra repayment as its own budget item (Savings → Debt payoff). Book one-time extra repayments directly on the debt.
glossary.schneeball.title: Snowball method
glossary.schneeball.short: Pay off the smallest debt first, then move its payment to the next one – quick wins.
glossary.schneeball.text: All debts get their minimum payment, extra money goes to the smallest balance. Once it is paid off, its payment rolls over to the next. Early successes keep you motivated.
glossary.lawine.title: Avalanche method
glossary.lawine.short: Pay off the debt with the highest interest rate first – mathematically the cheapest strategy.
glossary.lawine.text: Like the snowball, but the extra money is directed to the most expensive loan. This usually saves the most interest.
glossary.zinsbindung.title: Fixed-rate period
glossary.zinsbindung.short: The period for which a mortgage interest rate is fixed.
glossary.zinsbindung.text: At the end of the fixed-rate period a remaining balance usually remains, which is refinanced at the then current conditions.
glossary.leasing.title: Lease and residual value
glossary.leasing.short: A monthly usage payment for a fixed term; at the end a final payment (residual value) may be due.
glossary.leasing.text: In BudgetPlaner a lease is tracked as a liability without interest: the remaining balance equals the open payments plus the residual value.
glossary.dispo.title: Overdraft
glossary.dispo.short: The overdraft facility of your current account – usually with high interest.
glossary.dispo.text: A permanently used overdraft is expensive. A buffer as a cushion and a look at the cash-flow calendar help to avoid it.
glossary.vermoegen.title: Net worth
glossary.vermoegen.short: Sum of all buffers minus sum of all remaining debts.
glossary.vermoegen.text: The net-worth history shows over at least twelve months how savings and debts develop together.
glossary.zinseszins.title: Compound interest
glossary.zinseszins.short: Interest on interest already earned – money grows exponentially, not linearly.
glossary.zinseszins.text: The earlier and more regularly you save, the stronger the effect. The compound interest calculator shows the development over the years.
glossary.inflation.title: Inflation and purchasing power
glossary.inflation.short: Rising prices reduce what you can buy later with the same amount.
glossary.inflation.text: At 2% inflation, 100,000 in 20 years is only worth about 67,300 in today’s purchasing power. The calculators can show the real (inflation-adjusted) development.
glossary.guiltfree.title: Guilt-free
glossary.guiltfree.short: Money you may spend on joy without a bad conscience – eating out, hobbies, trips.
glossary.guiltfree.text: A fixed guilt-free amount makes a budget workable in everyday life: what is planned here, you may enjoy.
glossary.geben.title: Giving
glossary.geben.short: Donations, gifts and support for others – planned on purpose.
glossary.geben.text: Planning to give shows how much is possible without straining the rest of the budget.
glossary.investieren.title: Investing
glossary.investieren.short: Long-term wealth building, e.g. with an ETF savings plan.
glossary.investieren.text: Investing belongs to the savings group. An emergency fund should come first, and expensive debts should be paid off.
glossary.szenario.title: Scenario simulation
glossary.szenario.short: “What if …?” – try out changes without touching real data.
glossary.szenario.text: In a scenario you can simulate e.g. a salary change, a new expense or a higher loan payment. The forecasts update instantly. “Discard” resets everything exactly.
glossary.prognose.title: Forecast
glossary.prognose.short: A projection based on your plan, e.g. account balance, becoming debt-free or a savings goal.
glossary.prognose.text: Forecasts use the planned items of the coming months. Savings goal forecasts use the average of the last three months including the current plan.
glossary.engpass.title: Bottleneck
glossary.engpass.short: A month in which your account balance is expected to drop below zero.
glossary.engpass.text: The balance forecast marks bottlenecks in the next twelve months – often caused by yearly payments such as insurance.
glossary.schuldendienst.title: Debt service ratio
glossary.schuldendienst.short: Monthly loan payments ÷ income. Green up to 20%, yellow up to 35%.
glossary.schuldendienst.text: The higher the ratio, the less room remains for savings and the unexpected.
glossary.haushalt.title: Household
glossary.haushalt.short: The shared budget unit – several people see and edit the same data.
glossary.haushalt.text: The owner manages members and settings (currency, month start). Members edit the budget data. Changes appear in real time on all devices.
glossary.magiclink.title: Magic link
glossary.magiclink.short: A time-limited, single-use sign-in link by email – instead of a password.
glossary.magiclink.text: The email also contains a 6-digit code. Both are valid for 15 minutes and can be used only once.
glossary.passkey.title: Passkey
glossary.passkey.short: Sign in with Face ID, fingerprint or device code – without a password and without email.
glossary.passkey.text: You set up a passkey once in your profile. The secret key never leaves your device.
glossary.pwa.title: Install the app (PWA)
glossary.pwa.short: BudgetPlaner can be installed on your home screen without an app store and then also works offline.
glossary.pwa.text: Android/Chrome: menu → “Install app”. iPhone/Safari: Share → “Add to Home Screen”. Afterwards the app starts without an address bar and can receive push notifications.
glossary.zielzone.title: Target zone
glossary.zielzone.short: Shows how close your Unassigned is to 0.
glossary.zielzone.text: If the marker is in the middle, every euro has a job. Left means overplanned, right means money is still to be distributed.
glossary.sollzins.title: Interest rate
glossary.sollzins.short: Annual rate you pay on the remaining debt.
glossary.sollzins.text: The (nominal) interest rate is the yearly rate applied to the remaining debt. BudgetPlaner calculates monthly with rate ÷ 12 on the current remaining debt. The annual percentage rate (APR) also includes fees and is therefore slightly higher – for the amortization calculation the nominal rate counts.
